reasoning: All 15 edits are kept. Their targets exist in the current skill, none touch the protected slow-update block, and the failure and success edits do not contradict each other. Failure edits come first and are unchanged. They are the pronoun and title referent rule, the qualified-variant rule, the era granularity rule, the plural fruit/crop rule, the last-step short-form check, and the corporate-suffix rule with its partnership exception. The success edits cover patterns the failure edits do not: definition-style headwords, shared titles for lists of real people, contestant-response and article stripping, host asides, aggregator page titles, truncated archive hits and '___' blanks, keeping the full standard term for 'type of' clues, counting/ordinal clues, and 'varieties of this <noun>' clues. The two groups are consistent on overlapping ground. The failure rule to strip a qualifier the clue supplies ('Bagpipes', not 'Great Highland Bagpipe') agrees with the success rule to keep the head noun of a fixed term ('drip irrigation'). The failure short-form check and the existing 'Studio 60' guidance say the same thing, so nothing is dropped. Two edits (the pronoun rule and the counting rule) insert after the same 'One of these <role/title>' line. Both are additive, so order does not matter.

edits.target: - 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - Pronoun-led clues ('She played Tina Turner on the big screen & Rosa Parks on TV', 'He wrote...', 'Her home is now a museum', 'The 1815 Treaty of Paris was signed after his final defeat at Waterloo') ask for the PERSON (or group) the pronoun stands for, even without 'this'. A work, role, film, character, place, treaty, battle or event named in the clue or passages is evidence, never the answer. Find the person every passage ties to ALL the listed roles or deeds and give the plain 'First Last' name ('Angela Bassett', not 'What's Love Got to Do with It'; 'Napoleon', not 'Treaty of Paris'). A bare '<Title> <Full name>' clue ('Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah', 'President X', 'Prime Minister Y') asks for the country or body he led ('Brunei'), not 'Sultan of Brunei', the title or his name.

edits.target: Other clue details (diet, ingredient, cooking method) are just conditions on the generic dish.
edits.content: - Qualified-variant clues ('The Highland version of this instrument has a blowpipe, a chanter & 3 drones'; 'Rubber is an ingredient in this type of chewing gum'; 'the rare passing in front of the sun that Venus did'): the answer is the standard name of the category the clue points to, with the clue's own qualifier removed. 'Highland version of this instrument' -> 'Bagpipes' (not 'Great Highland Bagpipe'). 'The rare passing ... that Venus did' -> 'Transit' (not 'Transit of Venus'). 'This type of chewing gum' needs a NAMED type ('bubble gum'). A descriptive adjective copied from a passage ('synthetic') does not name a type, so look for the type name the passages use (a title like 'How It's Made - Bubble Gum'). Check the candidate contains no word the clue already supplies as a qualifier.

- Granularity: a clue with no pointer word that is only a person plus a charge, deed or event ('Henry Ward Beecher, for adultery') often comes from a category whose answer is the umbrella era the passages place it in (century, decade, period). Passages repeating one year ('1875 trial') are just evidence. Answer at the coarser level ('the 19th century'), keeping a leading 'the', not the specific year.

edits.target: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas') or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'.
edits.content: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'. A fruit, vegetable, grain, nut or flower named as the theme of a festival, harvest, market or industry ('the Oxnard festival for this fruit') takes the PLURAL ('Strawberries', 'Apples', 'Bananas'), as do plural-only things ('Bagpipes', 'Scissors').

edits.target: Brief reasoning belongs before the tags.
edits.content: - LAST-STEP SHORT-FORM CHECK (run it on your final candidate): cut any tagline or subtitle ('X on the Sunset Strip', 'X: The Movie'), any league, brand or organization prefix on a generic sport, game or item ('NFL football' -> 'Football'; 'MLB baseball' -> 'Baseball'), and any category noun the clue already supplies ('sport', 'show', 'film'). For 'this sport / this game' the answer is the sport's own bare name, even when the passages give league-specific measurements or rules. Trivia keys list 'Studio 60' and 'Football', not the long forms.

Drop corporate suffixes ('McCormick', not 'McCormick & Company'; also drop Inc., Corp., Co., Ltd., '& Sons'), even when the passage titles print the full legal name. For 'this spice company / this airline / this brand' answer with the bare brand name. Exception: a blank inside a famous partnership ('Publishing partners: ___ & Wagnalls', 'Partners: ___ & Jerry') asks for the full pair name as a trivia key lists it ('Funk & Wagnalls'), not the single missing word.

edits.target: and answer with the common English name (Conch).
edits.content: - Definition-style clues ('Sickle-shaped weapon of the Australian Aborigines', 'the sound a small object makes dropping into water, sometimes without a splash') have no 'this' pointer. Find the dictionary or encyclopedia page whose text paraphrases the clue ('the characteristic sound made by an object dropping into water without a splash'). The headword in its title ('Plop - definition of plop', 'Boomerang - Wikipedia') is the answer. Give that bare headword, without the category words the clue supplies ('sound', 'weapon'). A headword that recurs across several page titles beats a one-off word from a single passage.

edits.target: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
edits.content: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state, realm or other entity they share. A clue such as 'Title held in different countries at different times by Balbinus, Bao Dai & Bidatsu' asks for the shared title or role as a bare common noun ('Emperor'), not a country, one person, or the list items.

edits.target: Do not lengthen it with descriptors ('Madge', not 'Madge the Manicurist').
edits.content: Archive answers may be written as a contestant response ('"What is France?"', 'Who is Wally Lamb?') or with a leading article ('a bouncer', 'a fall', 'the harpsichord'). Strip the 'What is / Who is' wrapper and the leading a/an/the (unless the article is part of a proper title) and answer with the bare entity ('France', 'bouncer', 'fall').

edits.target: The archived clue may be slightly garbled (missing accents or letters, parentheses, dropped words), so match on the distinctive words.
edits.content: Video or host asides at the start of a clue ('(Jimmy of the Clue Crew grapples with another clue...)') may or may not be reproduced in the archive. Match on the factual core after the aside ('the shoulders have to be pinned to the mat for 1 second...').

edits.target: Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content: - Aggregator pages (Search-ID, flashcard or quiz-site pages) often put the answer in the PAGE TITLE, with the clue repeated verbatim in the snippet ('fall - Search-ID.com' over a snippet repeating the clue; '[TLE] lenin - Search-ID [PAR] ...In 1927, this Russian leader's book "The State & Revolution" was banned in Boston...'). Treat a short title word that sits over a snippet containing the clue's distinctive words as the prime candidate ('fall', 'Lenin'), and sanity-check it against the clue. This works even when the context is only two short passages.

edits.target: Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - When the clue appears verbatim only in page titles or snippets that stop before any answer, do not give up. Read the other passages for lines that restate the clue's descriptors next to a named entity ('Geppetto is a poor, lonely wood carver'; tags such as 'edna st vincent millay, bluebeard'). Combine that with your own knowledge and answer with that entity. An explicit '___' blank in the clue works like a slot: take the word that fills the same position in the phrase the passages repeat ('Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure' -> 'Transportation').

edits.target: The 'do not repeat clue words' rule is for a separate modifier already stated in the clue ('hasty' + pudding).
edits.content: - 'Type/kind of <noun>' and 'this <dish/rank/term>' clues where the passages repeat one fixed two-word term: keep the whole standard term when the bare modifier alone is not the thing asked for or is ambiguous. 'The type of irrigation used in Israel to make the desert bloom' -> 'drip irrigation' (not 'drip'). 'Southern pie with an insect name, green, cookie-crumb crust' -> 'Grasshopper pie' (not 'Grasshopper', which is just an insect). 'rise 5 ranks from Tenderfoot & you're one of these' -> 'Eagle Scout'. Strip only a modifier the clue itself supplies, never the head noun of the standard term.

edits.target: asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - Counting or ordinal clues ('rise 5 ranks from Tenderfoot & you're one of these', 'the third ... after X'): find the passage that lists the full ordered sequence (Scout, Tenderfoot, Second Class, First Class, Star, Life, Eagle), count from the anchor named in the clue, and answer with the item you land on, using the form the passages use ('Eagle Scout'). Do not answer with the anchor itself or a neighbouring step.

edits.target: - 'X needs A & one of these' / 'A, B and one of these': the clue already gives some members of a set. Find the passage listing the full set ('a subject and a predicate') and answer with the missing member ('subject'), never one already named in the clue.
edits.content: - 'X & Y are varieties / examples / types of this <noun>' ('Vermont & Tillamook are American varieties of this cheese'): X and Y are anchors, never the answer. Find the passage that names both together ('England supplies many fine Cheddars, as does Vermont and Tillamook') and answer with the shared generic noun in the singular ('Cheddar'). Use the shared noun, not one of the named items or a branded product.
